prize_parts.citation: For developing methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets and for dynamic models of industries, which made empirical industrial organisation a quantitative basis for market and policy analysis.

statement.case_for: B005 is the only shortlisted candidate that combines a cleanly attributable core, long validation and very wide use across fields. The random-coefficients demand framework (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) solved a specific, hard problem: how to estimate demand with endogenous prices and product characteristics while keeping a structural link to theory. Pakes's dynamic industry work extends this to entry, investment and competition over time. The tools are routine in merger review, antitrust and regulation, and are also used in trade, health and environmental economics. This is one of the clearest cases on the list of a measurement and identification advance that opened up new questions rather than just answering one. Three decades of adoption, refinement and critique mean the committee can judge lasting influence from evidence rather than expectation. Under common criteria that weigh originality, validated impact and clarity of credit, it ranks above candidates where credit is diffuse (B036), recent (B009) or dependent on contested cross-country identification (B014). I have not independently verified any of the facts in the opening files.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that B005 is a methods and estimation prize without a single headline substantive finding. The committee may weigh that against candidates that answer a first-order question about how economies work. Attribution also forces hard exclusions. Bresnahan and Reiss founded the new empirical IO tradition that preceded BLP. Benkard and Levin did significant dynamic-estimation work. Three names cannot cover all of this, and the choice of Levinsohn over Bresnahan is open to dispute. Structural estimates are also sensitive to functional-form, instrument and implementation choices, so the credibility of individual applications varies.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B005 first but would credit Bresnahan rather than Levinsohn alongside Pakes and Berry. He values Bresnahan's lead in inferring market power from data and notes that the three-name limit risks leaving out an important contributor.
responses.response: I take the Bresnahan point seriously and cannot dismiss it. The prize rationale is the point on which I come down differently. Bresnahan's new-empirical-IO contribution is a conceptual and inferential programme that predates BLP. The step that made the programme usable with differentiated products and real price endogeneity is the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes estimator. I would build the citation around that identifiable method and its dynamic extension, which is why I keep Levinsohn. I would accept the opposite choice if colleagues judge that rewarding the earlier tradition is more faithful to how the field developed. Our difference is about what the citation is for, not about whether Bresnahan did important work.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B014 first. He argues that political economics gave a unified framework, from theory to systematic empirics, for how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape policy. He sees the field as mature and thoroughly tested, and he notes that the 2024 institutions prize may weigh against it.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and on the coherence of the programme, and I rank it second for those reasons. My reservation is about the identification standard. The 2024 recognition rested on a design that supports a causal reading, and the committee was reasonably explicit about that. The constitutional and electoral-rule evidence relies more on cross-country comparisons, which support a weaker causal claim. This is not a reason to exclude B014. It does lower my confidence relative to B005, where decades of use have tested the method directly. On overlap with 2024, I think the topics are distinct enough, because B014 concerns policy choice under rules rather than long-run prosperity. The committee should still expect to be asked why institutions are being recognised again so soon.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B027 first. He sees the collateral-constraint amplification mechanism as a foundation of macro-financial modelling, cleanly credited to Kiyotaki and Moore, fully mature and heavily used after 2008. He treats the Gertler-Gilchrist financial-accelerator line as tied to Bernanke's earlier recognition.
responses.response: I agree that Kiyotaki-Moore is a clean two-person attribution and that I would not extend it to Gertler or Gilchrist, which is why B027 is my third choice. I weigh it below B005 for two reasons. Direct empirical validation of the amplification mechanism is more indirect than the validation of the BLP toolkit, which has been exercised in thousands of applications and by regulators. The 2022 prize on banks and financial crises also covers adjacent ground. The conceptual originality is very high, and I would not be surprised if colleagues decided it should come first. I put it among the credible alternatives and not lower.

responses.point: Andersson also ranks B005 first. He flags the concern that it is a methods prize without a single headline substantive finding, and that the committee could credit Bresnahan or Reiss for the broader tradition.
responses.response: I share the concern but do not think it counts decisively against B005. The measurement contribution is itself the discovery, because it made a class of questions answerable that were not answerable before. Those questions include price elasticities in differentiated markets, welfare effects of mergers and the value of new products. The test I would apply is the same for every candidate: did it change what the profession can credibly know, and has that been validated in use? B005 passes on both counts. I also see a risk of treating methods as lower-status on principle, which would disadvantage fields like this one relative to candidates with a clearer narrative.

uncertainties: Whether to credit Levinsohn or Bresnahan with Pakes and Berry. This depends on whether the citation rests on the BLP estimator or on the earlier new-empirical-IO tradition.

How much weight to give B014's weaker causal identification relative to its breadth and maturity, and whether the 2024 prize makes the committee reluctant to recognise institutions-related work this soon.
How to weigh a methods and measurement contribution against candidates with a more substantive headline finding, when the committee has no agreed way to compare them.
I have not verified independently any claims about prior prizes, citation counts or contribution dates. My assessments rest on the opening files and my own judgement.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for B005. For B014, my field (political science, democratisation and institutions) and my 2024 presentation speech on institutions are close to the topic, but the profile names no personal, collaborative or institutional tie to Persson, Tabellini or Besley. I share Stockholm University with IIES colleagues on this committee, in a different department. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it.
